answer: The policy number is PS 71-06, titled "Option and/or Major on Diploma." The CSULB Academic Senate published it, and the passage cites its minutes dated 1/15/71. It was deemed approved by the Academic Senate on 12/11/70 and approved by the President of the College on 1/6/71.

The Social Media policy is published by CSULB Strategic Communications. It is available at https://www.csulb.edu/social-media and covers user conduct and comments as well as university-generated content on the university's social media accounts.

The Policy on Student Organization Grants, published by Associated Students, Inc. (ASI) at California State University, Long Beach, governs how ASI awards money from the portion of its annual budget set aside for ASI Student Organization Program Grants and Travel Grants. It exists to give a fair and impartial basis for awarding these grants. The policy defines who is eligible, what types of programs and travel qualify, and how much can be awarded. Its purpose is to support student organizations in producing programs that meet the student body's needs and interests, and travel that supports professional, academic, and athletic development.

The policy describing the CSULB General Education Evaluation Committee (GEEC) is Policy Statement 22-07, published by the CSULB Academic Senate and available at https://www.csulb.edu/academic-senate/general-education-evaluation-committee-geec-1. Within the university's structure, the GEEC sits under the Institutional and Program Assessment Committee (IPAC), which must approve its policies and recommendations except for matters delegated to the GEEC itself. The GEEC also notifies the General Education Governing Committee (GEGC) of all its recommendations, as described in the Policy on General Education (PS 21-09). The passage does not give a physical location or contact details for the committee.

The CSULB Office of Equity and Compliance report covers the fiscal year from July 1, 2016 to June 30, 2017, so it is not recent and reflects data from that period only. The passage lists its date as July 1, 2016, which is the start of the reporting period rather than when the report was finished. Under CSULB's Misconduct in Research & Creative Activity policy (PS 16-01), the Complainant is responsible for making Allegations in good faith and for cooperating with both the Inquiry and the Investigation. As a matter of good practice, the Complainant should be interviewed at the Inquiry stage and given the typed notes or recording of the interview for correction. During an Investigation, the Complainant must be interviewed and must be given the typed notes or recordings of the interview for correction.

Under this section of the Policy on Volunteers, ASI recruits volunteers proactively to broaden campus involvement, without regard to gender, disability, age, race, sexual orientation, or other protected status, and the standard qualification is suitability to perform a task for the organization. Student volunteers must keep at least a 2.0 GPA each semester of service, must not be on probation of any kind, and must earn six units per semester (three units for graduate students), with additional requirements possible depending on the position. Volunteers may be recruited either for a specific position or out of general interest and later matched to a function. However, final acceptance cannot occur without a specific written position description for that volunteer.

The CSULB policy on Misconduct in Research & Creative Activity (PS 16-01) was approved by the President on February 1, 2016. The Academic Senate had recommended it at its meeting on December 5, 2015, and it was published by the CSULB Academic Senate. This policy supersedes PS 91-02.

Under this volunteer policy (published on asicsulb.org, the Associated Students site at CSULB), a position description must be written for each volunteer position and approved by the Human Resources Office before any volunteer is assigned or recruited. Each description must include the position's purpose and duties, a designated supervisor and worksite, a timeframe for the work, job qualifications, and job benefits. Descriptions must be reviewed and updated at least once a year, or whenever the work changes substantially. Each accepted volunteer receives the description, which is then used to manage and evaluate them, and HR is available to help staff develop these descriptions.

The CSULB Policy on Master's Level Program Culminating Activities, Policy Statement 25-12, supersedes three earlier policy statements: PS 95-07, PS 81-08, and PS 75-15. The Academic Senate recommended it on March 20, 2025, and the President approved it on April 11, 2025. It is dated April 12, 2025, and published by the CSULB Academic Senate.

Under the Policy on Complaint Management, all complaints, whether written or oral, receive equal regard and are investigated accordingly. Once a complaint is acknowledged, the Executive Director assigns the appropriate Division Director to investigate, unless the complaint involves that Director, in which case the Executive Director investigates personally. Within three working days of receiving the assignment, the Director must tell the complainant the timeframe for the investigation and for reporting results, and every attempt is made to finish the investigation and report within 30 calendar days. The investigating Director is given free and unrestricted access to all necessary records and premises, whether owned or rented, though the passage cuts off before listing any further provisions (source: https://asicsulb.org/corporate/documents/discover/policies/policy-on-complaint-management.pdf).

According to the ASI Bylaws 2025-26, each elected officer serves a term of no more than one year, ending on May 31. The term of office for these officers is set by each Board, subject to Senate approval. Officers may run for re-election an unlimited number of times. The exceptions are the President, Executive Vice President, and Vice President of Finance, who are limited to two years in the same position.

The Policy on Name Change of Schools to Colleges (PS 91-05) is posted at https://www.csulb.edu/academic-senate/policy-statement-91-05-name-change-of-schools-to-colleges-policy. It is published by the CSULB Academic Senate.

In the Policy on Student Research Fund, "activity" means the active process of collecting information and/or conducting research, typically guided by an earlier planning phase. This definition sets the application deadlines: students must apply no later than three weeks before research activity begins, or six weeks before if the research requires international travel. Grants cannot be awarded for research activity that is already in progress or completed.

CSULB's Office of Research and Economic Development (ORED) policy sets guidelines for using electronic or digital signatures in place of handwritten ones, as outlined by ICSUMA 08100.00 - Electronic and Digital Signatures. Digital signatures may be used for all internal processes, while some forms of electronic signatures may not suit certain workflows, although they are often easy to perform and acceptable in many cases. Only personnel with specific written delegation from the Board of Directors may enter contracts or sign documents on behalf of the CSULB Research Foundation. The document's purpose is to describe how to identify which forms and processes may use a specific type of electronic signature.

Although the section is titled "Maximum Units Allowed in a Major," the passage actually sets total unit requirements for the degree, not a cap on units within the major itself. Under PS 14-11, students pursuing a Bachelor of Arts or Bachelor of Science under graduation requirements established in or after the 2013-14 academic year must complete exactly 120 units, including at least 40 upper-division units or their equivalent, unless the Chancellor grants an exception. For the Bachelor of Fine Arts or Bachelor of Music under the same requirements, the degree must require between 120 and 132 units, or the limit set in Title 5, again unless the Chancellor grants an exception. The passage does not state a specific maximum number of units for a major.

CSULB Policy Statement 22-28, dated December 1, 2022, governs the voluntary reassignment of tenured and tenure-track faculty members to a new department, program, or other academic unit at their own initiative. It revises PS 96-09 and was approved by the Academic Senate on November 17, 2022, and by the President on November 28, 2022. Under the policy, any faculty member who has not received a notice of layoff may apply for permanent reassignment to another department or college, and no vacant position is required to apply. The faculty member must send a letter to the dean(s) of the affected college(s) describing their academic qualifications, their role in the new program, and their commitment to working with diverse students, faculty, and staff. The dean(s) then forward the letter and statement to the relevant academic unit chairs or directors.

The Selection and Term of Office of the NCAA Faculty Athletics Representative is covered by Policy Statement PS 26-06, dated May 5, 2026. This policy supersedes Policy Statement 95-02. The CSULB Academic Senate approved it on April 23, 2026, and the President approved it on April 29, 2026.

Policy Statement 73-18, issued by the CSULB Academic Senate, governs Foreign Study courses, which the institution offers as Summer Session classes through the Office of Summer Session or as Extension classes through the Office of Continuing Education. Each program is listed as Foreign Study 100, 200, 300, or 400, with departmental sponsorship specified for each class. Credit from a Summer Session offering counts as "in residence," while credit from an Extension offering is "extension credit." Students may apply no more than 12 units of Foreign Study credit toward a baccalaureate degree, and these courses can count toward major requirements only with the major department's approval. The policy also states that these courses are separate from the CSU International Programs "Year Abroad."

The Associated Students, Inc. (ASI) Policy on Complaint Management requires that all complaints against ASI or its employees be investigated and answered as quickly and thoroughly as circumstances allow, and resolved at the lowest possible level of the organization. Effective complaint handling is expected at every level, from the Executive Director to service delivery staff, and each ASI department must follow the policy. The policy does not discourage complainants from using other campus avenues, such as the Office of the Dean, Judicial Affairs, or University Police, and ASI will defer to the university's authority where appropriate and necessary. It does not cover complaints alleging discrimination, harassment, ethical violations, or fraud, or complaints from ASI employees or volunteers unless they are acting as ASI customers, since separate policies address those.

Under the Policy on Accounting, the Direct Payment procedure covers all payments not tied to a purchase order or contract, and invoices received by the Business Office are forwarded to the appropriate budget area contact to start the process. Purchases must follow ASI guidelines and be allowable under the funding source; otherwise the invoice will not be paid even if the goods were received, and the vendor will be told to seek payment from the individual who placed the order. The budget area must attach a completed Check Request, including the accounting distribution, to the original invoice. This request must be approved by someone listed on the budget area's Signature Authorization Card or Delegation of Authority Form, and no payment may be approved unless a current signature authorization record is on file in the A.S. Business Office. Completed Check Requests are then submitted to the A.S. Business Office for payment processing.

The Controlled Games section explains that casino nights, poker nights, and similar fundraisers held by nonprofit organizations, including auxiliary organizations, for charitable purposes are lawful under California Business and Professions Code §19985-19987, provided the nonprofit and any equipment or service suppliers submit an annual registration form to the Bureau of Gambling Control for approval 30 days before the event and check local police or sheriff reporting requirements. Each nonprofit may hold only one such event per year, lasting no more than five hours, and only people over 21 may participate. No cash prizes or wagers are allowed, but winners may receive donated prizes worth no more than $500 each, with a $5,000 total cap per event. At least 90 percent of gross revenue must go directly to the nonprofit, no more than 10 percent may compensate those running the event, and the games may not be conducted over the Internet. The passage also begins a sixth rule requiring detailed records for each event, but it is cut off before the details are given.

The policy (PS 11-06) was approved by the President, not by a collective body, on June 20, 2011. The Academic Senate recommended the revised policy on May 12, 2011, and the CSULB Academic Senate published it. It supersedes policies 79-18, 89-08, and 00-09.

According to the CSU Elections Handbook, the strict ban on using public funds and resources for political campaigns applies to issues before the voters. It does not limit the CSU's ability to take part in the legislative process, so state resources may be used for legislative advocacy. However, any position taken on behalf of the CSU must be approved by the Board of Trustees and facilitated through CSU Advocacy and State Relations, guided by the Statement of Legislative Principles the Board adopts at the start of each two-year session. Individual employees may advocate for bills important to a campus or system initiative, but they may not represent or imply that the CSU supports or opposes the bill. For federal matters, the Office of Federal Relations in Washington, D.C. coordinates priorities approved by the Board, and questions about state legislation can go to CSU Advocacy and State Relations.

This CSULB Academic Senate policy (PS 79-15) requires undergraduate students who enter with fewer than 56 transferable semester units to complete a one-unit course in order to graduate. The course covers the history, missions, and structures of American universities, use of the University Library, and career planning. Students must complete it during the first or second semester in which they enroll for more than six units of coursework (the passage prints this as "sic units," likely a typo for "six"). The Planning and Educational Policies Council is responsible for periodically reviewing the course, with an initial review during the 1984-85 academic year. The policy was approved in 1979, amended on April 30, 1984 and October 5, 1989, and took effect immediately.

Under Regulation XII: Insurance and Liability, students are generally individually responsible for any bodily injury, illness, or personal property loss or damage they incur while attending the University, and the University does not provide insurance coverage except in specific situations. This coverage supplements other health plans, pays only after them, covers accidents but not illness or disease, excludes treatment by CSU-employed or retained persons, and has a maximum benefit of $50,000 per covered person per accident.

The CSULB policy statement on implementing the federal Drug Free Schools and Communities Act Amendments of 1989 is PS 91-10, published by the CSULB Academic Senate. If the division or department does not approve the ongoing liability tied to the purchase, the CSULB Research Foundation Chief Operating Officer may grant an exception, and the asset may go to the CSULB Research Foundation instead. In the Subrecipient Policy, a sub-award is made to carry out a portion of a Federal award, and it creates a Federal assistance relationship with the sub-recipient (see §200.92 Subaward). Under 2 CFR 200.330, a sub-recipient does substantive work, unlike a contractor, which provides goods and services for the non-Federal entity's own use. Characteristics supporting sub-recipient classification include determining who is eligible to receive what Federal assistance and having its performance measured by whether the Federal program's objectives were met. The passage also notes that a sub-recipient normally provides critical project expertise that CSULB, as the PTE, does not possess, with a responsible investigator leading the work at the cooperating entity's site.

Under CSULB Policy Statement 22-22, the General Education Governing Committee (GEGC) has primary oversight of the General Education (GE) program. However, ultimate responsibility for approving GE courses and for creating and revising GE policy lies with the Curriculum and Educational Policies Council (CEPC), to which GEGC reports.

Under the ASI Policy on Banking, any funds handled on behalf of the ASI or its programs must be administered through bank accounts established in the name of the ASI or a CSULB Foundation. This policy implements Section 42403 of Title 5 of the California Code of Regulations, which requires that funds collected by or for a student body organization, except those from commercial services, be deposited in trust by the campus chief fiscal officer. Every bank account in the ASI's name must be authorized in advance by the Associate Vice President for Financial Management. No ASI program, function, or activity may establish or maintain an off-campus bank account without prior authorization from ASI and prior approval from the Associate Vice President for Financial Management.

Policy Statement 09-08, approved by the President on August 20, 2009 and superseding PS 75-07, covers Academic Renewal at CSULB. It allows an undergraduate student to petition to have all grades and units from one or two semesters (or up to three quarter terms) disregarded when computing grade point averages and academic standing, though no work from those terms may count toward baccalaureate requirements and all grades remain on record. To qualify, at least five calendar years must have passed since the work was completed, and the student must have since completed 15 semester units with a 3.0 GPA (or 30 units with a 2.5, or 45 units with a 2.0) at CSULB. The student must also have met, or be completing that semester, all graduation requirements other than GPA, and academic renewal cannot raise any GPA above what graduation requires.

Under CSULB's Misconduct in Research & Creative Activity policy (PS 16-01), if there is a final finding of no Research Misconduct and the Respondent(s) request it, the RIO must make all reasonable and practical efforts to restore the Respondent's reputation. Depending on the circumstances and the Respondent(s)' views, the RIO shall publicize the final outcome in any forum where the Allegation of Research Misconduct was previously publicized. Any institutional actions to restore the Respondent(s)' reputation should first be approved by the DO.

The CSULB Limited Submission Policy is available at https://www.csulb.edu/sites/default/files/document/limited_submission_policy_0.pdf. It is published by the CSULB Office of Research and Economic Development (ORED). The policy places responsibility on principal investigators to notify ORED of their intent to apply for a limited submission opportunity, and failure to follow its procedures may result in denial of approval for submission.

Policy Statement 06-04, published by the CSULB Academic Senate, addresses the declaration of a major and supersedes PS 97-09 and 02-08. To help ensure timely completion of graduation requirements, it requires students who have completed a total of 60 units to declare a major before they may register for the next term. It also requires upper-division transfer students to declare their intended major on their application for admission. The Senate recommended the policy on March 15, 2006, and the President approved it on March 23, 2006.

The CSULB Financial Conflict of Interest Policy (12/13/2017) sets guidelines for disclosing, identifying, and managing financial conflicts of interest for Investigators who design, conduct, or report research under a sponsored project or who propose one. The CSULB Office of Research and Sponsored Programs and the CSULB Research Foundation follow all federal, state, and California State University regulations when reviewing and managing FCOI disclosures. Although the university encourages researchers to work with industry and private ventures, it recognizes that these ties can create conflicts between private interests and the public interest served by government funding. The policy therefore requires Investigators on projects funded by non-governmental sponsors, the NSF, the PHS, or other agencies adopting federal requirements to disclose all significant financial interests related to the proposed research.

CSULB's Timely Graduation for Undergraduates policy (PS 10-06), recommended by the Academic Senate on April 29, 2010 and approved by the president on May 17, 2010, aims to ensure timely graduation so that as many qualified students as possible can access undergraduate programs. Students may earn up to 120% of the units required for their declared primary major, and any additional majors, minors, or certificates must fit within that limit. Transfer units beyond 60, along with units from AP, IB, other external exams, military credit, pre-baccalaureate credit, and credit by examination, do not count toward the limit. After earning 90 units, students may change degree objectives only by submitting a plan showing they can finish within the 120% limit of the higher-unit major. Students who have not filed to graduate by the time they reach 100% of their major's required units must file and submit a plan to graduate within the unit limits.

Policy Statement 26-05, which renames the CSULB College of Engineering as the Hung Family College of Engineering, is dated May 1, 2026. The Academic Senate recommended it on February 5, 2026, and the Provost approved it on May 1, 2026. The name change took effect immediately.

Under CSULB Policy Statement 25-15, section 2.1.1, an academic library department is defined as having a minimum of six tenured or tenure-track faculty librarians, at least three of whom must be tenured. This parallels the general department definition, which also requires six tenured or tenure-track faculty with three tenured. Unlike the general definition, however, the library department definition does not mention a requirement for a major recognized by the U.S. Department of Education.

The CSULB Policy on Master's Degrees (PS 25-11) is available at https://www.csulb.edu/academic-senate/policy-masters-degrees. It was published by the CSULB Academic Senate and approved by the President on April 11, 2025.

The Independent Studies Courses policy is covered by Policy Statement (PS) 08-08, dated March 3, 2008. The Academic Senate recommended it on February 14, 2008, and the President approved it on February 29, 2008. It supersedes APL 76-26 and PS 83-05 and 94-06.

Although the passage is labeled "Repetition of Courses (PS 23-24)," its content comes from the University RTP Policy and does not address course repetition. It states that each college RTP policy must specify in writing the standards for evaluating candidates in all three areas of evaluation, consistent with the university RTP policy, and must ensure consistency of standards across the college while reflecting the breadth of its disciplines. The college policy must be ratified by a majority of voting tenure-track and tenured college faculty, approved by the dean and the provost, and regularly reviewed by the college's tenure-track and tenured faculty. The college RTP committee reviews the candidate's materials and the department-level evaluations, applies department, college, and university standards, ensures fair and consistent evaluation, and must take seriously into account the department's specific standards.

Under the General Provisions for Goods, the Contractor must obtain and maintain three required coverages: Comprehensive or Commercial Form General Liability Insurance, Business Automobile Liability Insurance, and Workers' Compensation including Employers Liability Insurance as required by law. The general liability policy must be on an occurrence basis, cover bodily injury, personal injury, property damage, and contractual liability, and have an aggregate limit that applies separately to the Work. The automobile policy, also on an occurrence basis, must cover owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles for bodily injury, property damage, and contractual liability, including uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage. The Contractor may also be required to carry Environmental Impairment Liability Insurance if the Work involves hazardous materials such as asbestos, lead, fuel storage tanks, or PCBs, as well as other insurance agreed upon with the Long Beach State Foundation.

In CSULB's F&A rate guidelines, "life" refers to the life of a sponsored agreement and is interpreted as each competitive segment of a project. A competitive segment is a period of years approved by the Federal funding agency at the time of the award. Under 2 CFR 200 Appendix III (C)(7), the negotiated F&A rates in effect at the time of the initial award are used throughout that life. If the negotiated rate agreements don't extend through the full life of the agreement, the rate for the last year is extended through its end.

The CSULB Graduation Writing Assessment Requirement Committee (GWARC) Charge and Membership, Policy Statement 26-03, is dated March 23, 2026. The policy defines the philosophy, goal, objectives, responsibilities, and purposes of the university's undergraduate academic advising program.

According to ASI's Policy on Procurement, price is not always the deciding factor: payment terms, product quality, compatibility with existing equipment, and delivery schedules can matter more. Because ASI receives federal funds, it is encouraged to make purchases from "disadvantaged" businesses, including minority-owned, disabled veteran-owned, women-owned, and small businesses. ASI has obtained local and statewide directories of such businesses, and departments are encouraged to use them to identify vendors. The ASI Business Office also purges the Supplier List each year of vendors ASI no longer does business with or chooses to avoid.

Under Section 10.1, the "Use of Grant Funds" section of the Policy on Student Organization Grants says that ASI-funded organizations must request reimbursement or payment from their ASI grants by completing the required forms. Under the Policy on Agency Accounts, agency funds may not be used to open or maintain off-campus or other unauthorized bank accounts. To enforce this, checks drawn on an agency account will never be made payable to the organization itself or to any of its officers. The one exception is that a check may be made payable to an officer when it reimburses legitimate, documented organization expenses.

Under CSULB Policy Statement 81-07, one Continuing Education Unit (CEU) equals ten contact hours of participation in an organized continuing education experience under responsible sponsorship, capable direction, and qualified instruction. The CEU measures noncredit continuing education activities, courses, and programs, including independent and informal study. A decimal fraction of a CEU may be awarded when appropriate, but no less than .5 CEU per program, and only complete instructional hours count, so 18.5 contact hours would earn at most 1.8 CEU. CEUs may be awarded for up to 8 hours of instruction per day if students have no work commitment that day, or up to 4 hours per day after working hours.

Under section 6.2.1, once an investigation confirms a security breach involving notice triggering information, the CSULB Office of Information Security Management and Compliance must notify the Vice President of Administration and Finance and the Office of General Counsel. If the breach is large enough that a press release may be needed, that office also notifies the Senior Director, Information Security Management, the Associate Vice President, University Relations, and the Office of the Chancellor, with a copy to the CIO/Assistant Vice Chancellor. The office then confirms the breach with the responsible department and gives it advice and guidance. It also starts the campus breach notification process, works with the Executive Director or designee responsible for the breached electronic equipment to handle the response and inquiries, and guides the employees designated to answer breach notification inquiries.

The passage from PS 16-04 does not define "FAA" or spell out the acronym. The Jeanne Clery Disclosure of Campus Security Policy and Crime Statistics Act (20 USC § 1092(f)) is a federal law, not a CSULB policy, that requires colleges and universities nationwide to disclose information about crime on and around their campuses. It is named in memory of Jeanne Ann Clery, a 19-year-old Lehigh University freshman who experienced Clery reportable crimes in her residence hall room in April 1986. Under this law, the CSULB University Police publish an Annual Security Report that gives notice of campus crime statistics and shares safety and prevention information with the community. The report reflects California State University, Long Beach's stated commitment to a safe and secure environment for students, faculty, staff, and guests.

According to the Policy on General Education (PS 21-09), the General Education Program teaches students a broad base of knowledge from a variety of disciplines. This prepares them to lead engaged and meaningful lives that exemplify CSULB's values of intellectual rigor, inclusive excellence, and the public good. Students complete GE alongside their major, which focuses on discipline-specific education and sometimes prepares them for specific professions. In the liberal arts tradition, GE introduces students to new areas and gives them knowledge and skills that may or may not relate to their disciplines, rather than primarily complementing the major or catering to their preexisting interests.

The Establishment of Student Department Association is covered by Policy Statement PS 71-01. The passage notes that this policy was published by the CSULB Academic Senate and is recorded in the minutes of 1/15/71 as AS (SA) 71-1. It serves as the basis for deciding which departmental student association the Associated Students recognize for funding when there is a dispute over representation.

CSULB's Care & Protection of Personal Property on Campus policy (PS 92-11), published by the CSULB Academic Senate, recognizes that employees routinely keep books, notes, teaching aids, office machinery, and other personal property in their assigned offices, laboratories, and work spaces, often because these items are essential to their professional effectiveness. The university commits to safeguarding such property and prohibits transferring or removing it without the owner's consent except under extenuating circumstances. The policy also requires that employees be notified of pending remodeling, construction, and major routine maintenance projects affecting their offices so they can remove items or otherwise arrange for their care. When access to offices is needed for a department-requested Plant Operations service order rather than a contract remodeling or construction project, the individual who authorized the service order is responsible for giving preliminary notice to the affected employees.

The Academic Centers and Institutes (ACI Policy), Policy Statement 14-04, supersedes three older policy statements: PS 92-03, PS 97-06, and PS 98-10. The Academic Senate recommended it on February 6, 2014, and the President approved it on April 1, 2014. It is dated April 14, 2014.

The Independent Contractor Agreement, published by the Long Beach State Foundation, is a template contract between the Foundation and a contractor, with blanks for the date, city, county, contract term, and payment amount. Under Article 1, the agreement runs for a specified term unless it is terminated under the provisions of Article 7. Article 2 states that the Foundation will pay the contractor an agreed sum for the services described in Section 4.01. The contractor must submit detailed invoices and provide a completed Form W-9 with the first invoice. The contractor is also responsible for all costs of performing the services, including equipment, staff and subcontractor costs, fees, fines, licenses, bonds, and taxes, and the Foundation will not cover any of the contractor's expenses. CSULB Academic Senate Policy Statement 07-01, the Student Grievance Policy dated January 26, 2007, supersedes PS 95-06 and PS 95-21. The Academic Senate recommended it on November 2, 2006, and the President concurred on November 14, 2006. It provides a formal, standardized way for students to seek redress for unauthorized or unjustified actions by faculty, administrators, or staff that adversely affect their status, rights, or privileges.

According to the Policy on Signature Authorization, the Executive Director may revoke the signature authority of any Division Director or department supervisor. This can happen when the Executive Director and Treasurer determine that the signatory has engaged in an improper transaction as defined in the policy. It can also happen when they determine that the signatory lacks sufficient knowledge of the current policies, rules, laws, regulations, and other restrictions on the use of the resources for which he or she has been delegated authority. Once revoked, signature authority may be reinstated only with the approval of the Executive Director and Treasurer.

Under CSULB's Discontinuance of Academic Programs policy (PS 11-05), when a request to discontinue an academic program is received, the Vice-President for Academic Affairs initiates a program discontinuance study (Section 1.400). The study can be skipped, and the request sent directly to the appropriate University Councils, if the initiating body shows evidence of one or more specific conditions (Section 1.300). These conditions are: no students enrolled in the previous three years; demand so low that necessary courses haven't been offered in three years; an alternate program in the same unit better serves student needs; needed faculty have left and long-range planning favors hiring in other areas; or an external agency, such as a credentialing or accreditation body, required discontinuance. Even in those cases, a study must still be carried out if any three people (students, faculty members, or administrators) request one.

The Mission Statement for CSU, Long Beach (PS 90-00), published by the CSULB Academic Senate, describes CSULB as a large urban comprehensive university in the California State University system. Its mission is to provide high-quality education leading to a broad range of baccalaureate and master's degrees in the liberal arts and sciences and many applied and professional fields, with emphasis on upper-division and graduate instruction, in accordance with the California Master Plan for Higher Education. Committed to serving the people of California and to assuring access and equity, the University tries to serve evening and daytime students, part-time and full-time students, and students from groups with both historically lower and historically higher rates of enrollment. It serves graduates in the top third of the State's high school graduating class, community college transfers, and adults reentering education.

In PS 22-13, "Term of Temporary Appointments" (section 6.3) sets how long an interim or acting academic administrator may serve. The temporary appointee serves until the effective date of the permanent appointment or the date the permanent appointee reports for duty, whichever is later, but the term may not exceed one year. Under 6.3.1, the appointment can be extended for an additional six months only after consultation with the appropriate constituencies and after a written justification is provided to them. For university-wide positions and College Deans, that constituency is the Academic Senate Executive Committee, and for other college positions it is the Faculty Councils.

The memo, dated March 26, 2013, and issued by Academic Senate Chair Daniel J. O'Connor, records that the CSULB Academic Senate Executive Committee unanimously approved an interpretation of Senate Policy Statement 11-06, Section 6.0, in consultation with Robert's Rules of Order. Section 6.0 covers how a department recommends department chair candidates to the dean: after nominations, the nominating committee chair prepares and distributes ballots to eligible faculty with a return deadline of ten working days. Eligible faculty vote by secret ballot, marking each nominee "recommended," "not recommended," or abstaining, and blank ballots do not count as votes cast. Faculty on authorized leave receive ballots by first-class mail or email, returning a hard copy in a sealed envelope, and the nominating committee counts and reports the results. The passage cuts off before stating the actual interpretation, so its specific ruling cannot be determined from this text.

Under CSULB Policy Statement 10-10, the candidate submits the entire research, scholarly, and/or creative work section of the RTP file to the Office of Faculty Affairs, which forwards it to each external evaluator. Each evaluator is asked to report on the quality and overall impact of the candidate's submitted materials on the discipline or profession, but not to recommend for or against the RTP action under consideration. The AVP for Faculty Affairs informs evaluators that their reports will be included in the candidate's RTP file and that the candidate will receive a copy. Each level of review treats these reports as additional evidence and considers them along with all other evidence in the file.

Regulation XVIII, published by CSULB Student Affairs, states that the CSU prohibits Discrimination, including Harassment, based on any Protected Status. These statuses include Age, Disability, Gender, Gender Identity, Gender Expression, Genetic Information, Marital Status, Medical Condition, Nationality, Pregnancy, Race or Ethnicity, Religion, Sex, Sexual Orientation, and Veteran or Military Status. Under the Policy on Master's Degrees (PS 25-11), a full-time academic load for a graduate student in a master's degree program is 8 units per semester, and the maximum load is 18 units per semester. A student who wishes to exceed this 18-unit limit must first meet with their Graduate Advisor. The CSU Elections Handbook, published by CSULB Government Relations, is a general reference guide to issues that have come up within the CSU about using state resources in elections, along with guidance on other election questions. Its central principle is that the law prohibits using public funds for political campaign activity, as established in *Stanson v. Mott* (1976), which held that a public agency may not spend public funds to promote a partisan position in an election campaign. It also cites Government Code section 8314, which makes it unlawful for state officers, appointees, employees, or consultants to use or allow others to use state resources for unauthorized campaign activity. The handbook ties this campaign neutrality rule to Education Code § 66607, which requires the CSU to remain "entirely independent of all political and sectarian influence," and to the California Constitution's ban on gifts of public funds.

Under the Policy on Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation, dating violence is abuse committed by a person who is or has been in a social or dating relationship of a romantic or intimate nature with the victim. This can include someone the victim just met, such as at a party, through a friend, or on a social networking website. "Abuse" means intentionally or recklessly causing or attempting to cause bodily injury, or placing another person in reasonable apprehension of imminent serious bodily injury to themselves or others. It does not include non-physical, emotional distress or injury.

Under the Cost Transfers policy, a cost transfer is any transfer of expenditures to or from a sponsored project (an LBFDN G fund) to align costs with the actual benefit the project received. Any penalties, disallowances, or loss of funding caused by non-compliance will be assessed against the department that violated the policy. The Principal Investigator or a designee is expected to review the fiscal status of sponsored project accounts regularly, with monthly review recommended, and to promptly request corrections for incorrectly recorded expenses. The CSULB Research Foundation also recognizes that transfers between sponsored project accounts are occasionally necessary to correct bookkeeping or clerical errors in the original charges.

Under CSULB's PS 19-03, reassigned time releases faculty from other duties to pursue research, scholarly, and creative activity (RSCA), while faculty small grants are monetary awards that can cover expenses like student assistance, minor equipment, materials and supplies, or RSCA-related travel. Both are awarded competitively at the college level, using Academic Affairs allocations that colleges may supplement with their own funds. Awards may take the form of reassigned time, small grants, or a combination, equivalent to the Vacant Rate for up to 6 WTU per academic year. Requests above 3 WTU require additional justification, and awardees receiving more than 3 WTU of reassigned time may take it in one semester or spread it over two. College faculty councils set the application and evaluation criteria, procedures, and deadlines, determine the award committee's composition and charge, and may establish procedures for converting reassigned time into small grants and vice versa.

Under CSULB Academic Senate Policy Statement 73-03 (March 4, 1974), non-matriculating students may enroll in regular program classes by paying extension fees, provided there is insufficient enrollment to develop an extension class and the department concerned grants permission. Funds from concurrent enrollment are divided as follows: 25 percent to the Continuing Education Reserve Fund, 50 percent to supporting departments on a pro rata basis, and 25 percent to the Office of Continuing Education for operating expenses. The policy also incorporates Chancellor's Office rules: extension students cannot justify continuing a low-enrollment class, take a place from a resident student, or be a reason for splitting a class. Concurrent enrollment should cause no loss to the Continuing Education Revenue Fund, which must keep a reasonable percentage to cover indirect costs, and any revenue beyond what extension needs to run the program may be spent for other University purposes.

Under CSULB's University RTP Policy (PS 23-24), all tenure-track and tenured faculty undergo performance review: tenure-track faculty are evaluated every year, with a periodic review in years without reappointment, tenure, or promotion review, and tenured faculty are evaluated every five years. For assistant professors appointed without service credit, the first- and second-year evaluations are periodic reviews that give feedback on progress toward tenure. These reviews are conducted by the department RTP committee, department chair, and college dean, although the first-year review may involve only the chair and dean. In the third year, the evaluation is a reappointment review, and successful candidates are reappointed for one, two, or three years. In the fourth and fifth years of continuous service, the annual evaluation is a periodic or reappointment review as appropriate, and actual timelines may vary with level of appointment and service credit.

CSULB Regulation XV prohibits gambling and lotteries on campus, at University functions, and by University organizations, because these activities are governed by California Penal Code Sections 330 through 337(s). Gambling includes any percentage game played with cards, dice, or another device for money, checks, credit, or anything else of value. Anyone who deals, plays, conducts, or bets on such games is guilty of a misdemeanor and may face a fine, imprisonment, University disciplinary action, or any combination of these sanctions.

Under the Policy on Cash Handling and Management (section 2.2.1), cash collection points are departments or other units that receive and handle cash on a regular basis. A department that wants to be designated as a cash collection point must request it from the Director of Finance and show it can follow appropriate cash handling procedures. Departments or units that handle cash receipts only occasionally must also follow the procedures and guidelines that apply to cash collection points.

The passage, which falls under the Engineering Controls section of the Policy on Hazard Communication Program, does not actually describe specific engineering controls. Compliance with those instructions is an essential part of worker training, and employers should make sure workers know what the words "danger," "warning," and "caution" mean and what they should do when they see them.

CSULB's Policy on Academic Internships (Non-Clinical/Non-Licensure), Policy Statement 24-21, sets guidelines for the university's student Academic Internship policy and procedures in response to Chancellor's Office Executive Order 1064. It affirms the educational value of internships and aims to maximize students' learning while reducing risks to participants and limiting the University's liability. The policy defines an Academic Internship as a faculty-approved and faculty-directed activity that combines academic study with supervised practical experience in business, nonprofit, government, educational, or other workplace settings. Because internships depend on outside organizations, CSULB cannot guarantee placements, and programs may require students to secure internship offers themselves.

The CSULB policy statement on academic progress rules is PS 11-10, "Academic Progress Rules for Undergraduate Programs," published by the CSULB Academic Senate (https://www.csulb.edu/academic-senate/policy-statement-11-10-academic-progress-rules). The Academic Senate recommended it on November 17, 2011, and the President approved it on November 30, 2011. It sets rules for departments to identify at-risk undergraduates who are not making sufficient progress so they can receive intervention. Identified students must meet with academic advisors to plan for completing their program, and if completion is not achievable, they are dismissed from that program and guided to a more appropriate one.

Under California Education Code 67380(a)(1)(A), CSULB must compile records of all crimes committed on campus that are reported to campus police, campus security personnel, or campus safety authorities, along with arrests for those crimes. This covers crimes involving violence, hate violence, theft, destruction of property, illegal drugs, or alcohol intoxication. The university must make this information available within two business days when students, prospective students, employees, or the media request it. To request crime information, you can contact Chief John Brockie at john.brockie@csulb.edu.

Under CSULB policy, an electronic signature is an electronic sound (such as an audio file of a person's voice), symbol (such as a JPEG graphic representation of a person), or process (such as a procedure that conveys assent) that is attached to or logically associated with a record. It must be executed or adopted by a person with the intent to sign that record. Electronic signatures may be used for bilateral contractual and legal documents, unilateral contracts and other University and Research Foundation controlled documents, internal campus forms and approvals, and external forms and approvals.

Such a recommendation may also include recommendations for other appropriate actions, including administrative actions.

Under CSULB policy PS 22-13 (section 4.7), the search committee report is a document the search committee prepares containing its own confidential evaluation of the strengths and weaknesses of each candidate. The committee submits this report to the appointing authority, via the administrator to whom the appointee would report, along with a summary of the evaluations from the other interviewing constituencies and an unranked list of the three to five candidates it considers best qualified for appointment. If the appointing authority or that administrator disagrees with the committee's recommendations, they must meet with the committee to discuss the disagreement. The committee may then revise its report if it chooses.

The Deadline for Adding Classes and Implications of Adding Classes Late policy (PS 25-22) was approved by the President of California State University, Long Beach. Under the Academic Centers and Institutes (ACI) Policy (PS 14-04), an academic institute is a distinct and free-standing ancillary unit that may engage in a wide variety of scholarly and creative, instructional, and/or service activities, typically in areas of broad concern, but it does not offer for-credit instruction. Institutes are frequently interdisciplinary and may include personnel from multiple departments, schools, and colleges, even beyond campus boundaries. An institute coordinates and promotes faculty and student research and scholarly and creative activities on a continuing basis. It may also perform public service within the limits of its stated objectives.

Under the CSULB biological material transfer agreement, COMMERCIAL PURPOSES means the sale, lease, license, or other transfer of the MATERIAL or MODIFICATIONS to a for-profit organization. It also covers any organization's use of the MATERIAL or MODIFICATIONS, including the RECIPIENT's, to perform contract research, screen compound libraries, produce or manufacture products for general sale, or conduct research that results in such a transfer to a for-profit organization. Industrially sponsored academic research is not considered a commercial purpose per se unless one of those conditions is met.

Policy Statement 86-03, recommended by the CSULB Academic Senate on February 13, 1986, and approved by the President on February 27, 1986, aims to ensure instructional conditions that protect students' health and safety. It requires that students in specified laboratory and fieldwork courses be instructed in the safety rules, regulations, and practices for using laboratory materials, machinery, equipment, and other items the instructor identifies. Beginning in Fall 1986, each department, in consultation with the School Dean, decides which courses or sections the policy covers, and the list is kept in the Dean's and departmental offices. Students in those courses must receive safety instruction and sign a form certifying they received it, with copies given to both faculty and students. Faculty should also be able to verify student attendance at the safety instruction sessions.

CSULB Policy Statement 24-07, dated March 26, 2024, sets out the charge of the Committee on Athletics; it was approved by the Academic Senate on March 7, 2024, and by the President on March 21, 2024. The Committee serves as the primary advisory body to the Academic Senate and University administration on academic policy and philosophy for the Department of Athletics, and it is subordinate to the Academic Senate, to which it presents recommendations. It also serves as the primary advisory body to the Athletic Director on all University matters related to Athletics, and its members help promote Athletics across campus. Its specific functions include reviewing admission policies for athletes who do not meet regular admission requirements, as well as financial aid, retention, and educational equity.

Under CSULB's Time, Place and Manner policy, kiosks may be used only to promote campus events, activities, or programs sponsored by a Recognized Student Organization, a University-affiliated individual, or a University-affiliated department or group. Postings must meet the requirements in Section III. A1 and must state the event's name, date, time, location, and contact information (such as email or website), along with the date the material was posted. Each event is limited to 2 flyers or 1 poster per kiosk, with flyers no larger than 8½ x 11 inches and posters no larger than 17 x 22 inches. Material cannot go up more than 10 business days before the event and must be removed within 3 business days after it, though Recognized Student Organizations may post general meeting materials for up to 10 business days during the first four weeks of each semester.

The Policy on Injury and Illness Prevention Plan says that accidents, injuries, illnesses, and "near-misses" are investigated using procedures established in the plan, and their causes are identified and corrected. Supervisors also regularly monitor their work areas and correct or report potential safety hazards.

The passage is an excerpt from CSULB's Gift Acceptance Policy (dated March 24, 2024) under "General Policies," and it mainly covers endowment funds. Gifts that endow specific restricted purposes must be large enough to produce annual income sufficient to fulfill the donor's purposes indefinitely. To protect the fund, a substantial portion of the income should be returned to the principal, so endowment calculations normally assume a "spendable" income of a percentage of investment returns, consistent with Foundation Board policy, with the rest reinvested. Endowment funds are managed by the Foundation's Board of Directors according to the Foundation's investment and spending policies and California state law, and gift agreements also follow the Foundation's gift recognition policies.

The "Improper Transactions" section of the Policy on Signature Authorization says that anyone granted signature authority must not knowingly prepare or approve a business transaction that is incorrect, inappropriate, fraudulent, or in violation of ASI policies on fraud, conflict of interest, or employee conduct. Under CSULB Policy Statement 24-17, a certificate program is a coherent grouping of courses from one or more disciplines that provides a set of learning experiences, often but not always related to a specific career area, or alternatively a multidisciplinary focus on a specific topic or area. It differs substantially in focus and scope from a degree program, although certain common courses may apply to both. A certificate provides formal recognition by the University that the course of study involves substantial exposure to the discipline, topic, or area.

The Policy on Faculty Awards is Policy Statement 21-05 (PS 21-05) at California State University, Long Beach. It supersedes the earlier policy, PS 20-02. The Academic Senate recommended it on March 11, 2021, and the President approved it on March 24, 2021.

This sits alongside related requirements to notify the department of office hours by the end of the first week of instruction and to list office hours on each course syllabus.

Under CSULB Regulation X, recognized student, faculty, or staff organizations may use information tables to share information about their organization and its activities, provided the tabling does not unreasonably interfere with the campus's instructional program or operations or obstruct pedestrian or vehicular traffic. Each group or organization may hold such tabling events no more than four times a month. Reservations must be made with the Campus Events Office in PH1-103 at least 3 business days in advance, and same-day reservations are not allowed. Approval is required at least 1 business day in advance.
