CSULB Academic Senate Policy Statement 22-06, dated March 4, 2022, sets out the revised charge for the LGBTQIA+ Campus Climate Committee, a subcommittee of the general Campus Climate Committee. Its mission is to collaborate with all segments of the University to recruit, retain, and promote the success of LGBTQIA+ students, staff, faculty, and administrators, and its membership also includes allies. The committee supports educational programs that increase understanding of LGBTQIA+ and other diversity issues, preparing students for careers in diverse settings. Through partnerships with other cultural groups and organizations on campus, it advocates for all historically marginalized groups. Its specific responsibilities include performing periodic needs assessments of the campus climate regarding LGBTQIA+ issues, though the passage is cut off before listing the rest.

The CSULB policy statement on Requirements For Additional Baccalaureate Degrees (PS 11-01) supersedes policy 71-07. The Academic Senate recommended the revised policy on November 18, 2010, and the president approved it on December 8, 2010.

The passage dates Policy Statement 22-06, the revised charge for the LGBTQIA+ Campus Climate Committee, to March 4, 2022. It lists that date both in its header and alongside the policy statement number, and identifies the CSULB Academic Senate at California State University, Long Beach as the publisher. However, the passage does not explicitly say that March 4, 2022 is the approval date, so it could also be the date of issuance or publication.

Policy Statement 23-21, which renames the Department of Film and Electronic Arts as the Department of Cinematic Arts, is dated October 27, 2023. The CSULB Academic Senate approved the new title on October 19, 2023, and the CSULB Provost approved it on October 26, 2023. The name change takes effect in Fall 2024.

Under the Policy on Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation (source: asicsulb.org), stalking is a repeated Course of Conduct directed at a specific person that would cause a Reasonable Person to fear for their own or others' safety, or to suffer Substantial Emotional Distress. A Course of Conduct means two or more acts in which the stalker, directly, indirectly, or through third parties and by any means, follows, monitors, observes, surveils, threatens, or communicates to or about a person, or interferes with their property. A Reasonable Person is someone under similar circumstances and with the same Protected Status(es) as the complainant. Substantial Emotional Distress means significant mental suffering or anguish, which may, but does not necessarily, require medical or other professional treatment or counseling.

Yes, the Policy on Final Course Grades, Grading Procedures, and Final Assessments (PS 22-02) replaces earlier policies. It supersedes two prior policy statements, PS 09-07 and PS 12-03, and states that it complies with all relevant Executive Orders. The policy, dated January 3, 2022, was recommended by the CSULB Academic Senate on November 4, 2021, and approved by the President on December 13, 2021.

The Policies and Procedures for the Award of Honorary Degrees is Policy Statement 97-04 (PS 97-04), published by the CSULB Academic Senate. The Academic Senate recommended it on November 14, 1996, and the President approved it on December 19, 1996.

The policy number is PS 85-12, as the passage title states. The policy was recommended by the CSULB Academic Senate at its May 9, 1985 meeting and approved by the President on May 22, 1985. It is published by the CSULB Academic Senate at https://www.csulb.edu/academic-senate/policy-statement-85-12-faculty-early-retirement-program-ferp-pre-retirement.

The Department Policies are published by the CSULB University Police, as stated on the page at https://www.csulb.edu/university-police/department-policies. The passage explains that these California State University police department policies are developed using Lexipol, a policy management system based on constitutional law and nationally recognized best practices. The publicly accessible policies are posted to promote transparency and accountability and are routinely reviewed and updated.

Published by the CSULB Office of Research and Economic Development, this document sets terms for purchase orders for goods or services procured under federal awards, citing 2 C.F.R. § 200.327 and 2 C.F.R. Part 200, Appendix II. Contractors must comply with the applicable federal regulations for any purchase involving federal funds, as indicated on the purchase order cover sheet, and must pass applicable provisions down to lower-tier subcontractors. For contracts over $250,000, if deliverables or services fail to conform to the requirements or submitted samples, CSU may reject them. The contractor must then remove, correct, and replace them at no cost to CSU. If the contractor fails to do so, CSU may buy substitutes on the open market and deduct the cost from money owed to the contractor. The passage is cut off at that point.

The Policy on Student Media is published by Associated Students, Inc. (ASI). The passage doesn't name a specific office or department within ASI. It does say that ASI acts through its Student Media Board when it needs to show that disciplinary action is necessary, but it doesn't identify that board as the publisher.

You can read PS 21-03, the "Policy on Employment of Graduate Students as Student Assistants, Instructional Student Assistants, Graduate Assistants and Teaching Associates," at https://www.csulb.edu/academic-senate/employment-of-graduate-students-as-student-assistants-instructional-student. It is published by the CSULB Academic Senate at California State University, Long Beach. The policy is dated January 27, 2021, and supersedes Policy Statements 95-03, 96-21, and 17-18.

The memo, issued by the CSULB Academic Senate on January 25, 2023, gives the Executive Committee's interpretation of PS 20-01, the Policy on Online and Hybrid Instruction. It specifically addresses the phrase "essentially all" in Section 2.3, which defines face-to-face instruction as courses in which essentially all classroom instruction occurs synchronously with the instructor and students physically present. The Executive Committee found the phrase imprecise and potentially confusing for faculty, department chairs, program directors, and deans trying to apply the policy. It therefore concluded that College Deans may set a precise definition of "essentially all" for use in their own College.

The passage does not mention CSULB specifically; it comes from a CSU systemwide resource guide (calstate.edu). It defines the Orientation Checklist as a resource tool to help prepare service-learning students for their community engagement experience, which each campus can adapt for its various placements. The orientation should give students a clear understanding of the work they will do, its risks and preventions, and how to conduct themselves in the community as part of a class assignment. Some information applies to all students, while site-specific details come from conversations with the learning site, and responsibility may be shared or assigned to one party, such as the community partner.

Under CSULB's Time, Place and Manner policy, campus kiosks may be used only to promote campus events, activities, or programs sponsored by a Recognized Student Organization or a University-affiliated individual, department, or group. Postings must meet the requirements in Section III.A1 and must also state the event's name, date, time, location, contact information (such as email or website), and the date the material was posted. Each event is limited to 2 flyers (no larger than 8½ x 11 inches) or 1 poster (no larger than 17 x 22 inches) per kiosk. Material can go up no more than 10 business days before the event and must come down within 3 business days after it, although Recognized Student Organizations may post general meeting materials for up to 10 business days during the first four weeks of each semester.

Under PS 11-06, the dean may approve allocating department resources for one or more associate chairs, based on the department's size and complexity. The department chair is responsible for selecting associate chairs, in consultation with the department faculty. Associate chairs perform duties assigned by the department chair, but those duties may not include the chair's role in reappointment, tenure, and promotion (RTP) or in staff evaluations. Serving as associate chair does not entitle anyone to succeed to the department chair position.

Under CSULB Regulation X, recognized student, faculty, or staff organizations may use information tables to share information about their organization and its activities, provided the tabling does not unreasonably interfere with the campus's instructional program or operations or obstruct pedestrian or vehicular traffic. Each group or organization may hold such events no more than four times a month. Requesters must reserve with the Campus Events Office in PH1-103 at least 3 business days in advance, and same-day reservations are not allowed. Approval is required at least 1 business day in advance.

According to the ASI Bylaws 2025-26, all officers-elected or officers-designated assume their offices and duties on the first day of June or immediately after their appointment and its confirmation by the appropriate authority. The exception is Associate Justices designated under Article VII, Section 1.A.c. Officers filling vacancies by election or succession take office immediately once they meet all the requirements of their respective offices. All officers-elected must also take an Oath of Office upon Senate confirmation, swearing to be guided by the articles and bylaws of the Associated Students, Incorporated, and by integrity and principle so that all students are properly served.

According to the Policy on Complaint Management (https://asicsulb.org/corporate/documents/discover/policies/policy-on-complaint-management.pdf), all complaints, whether written or oral, are given equal regard and investigated. After acknowledging receipt, the Executive Director assigns the appropriate Division Director to investigate, unless the complaint involves that Director, in which case the Executive Director investigates personally. Within three working days of the assignment, the Director must tell the complainant the timeframe for the investigation and for reporting results, and every attempt is made to finish the investigation and report within 30 calendar days. The investigating Director gets free and unrestricted access to all necessary records and premises, whether owned or rented, though the passage cuts off before listing anything else the Director is provided.

Under CSULB's PS 11-05 (Discontinuance of Academic Programs), when a request to discontinue an academic program is received, the Vice-President for Academic Affairs must initiate a program discontinuance study (Section 1.400). Section 1.300 allows the study to be skipped, with the request going directly to the appropriate University Councils, if the initiating body presents evidence of at least one listed condition. These conditions are no student enrollment in the previous three years, demand so low that necessary courses haven't been offered in three years, an alternate program in the same unit that better serves students, departed faculty whose replacement the area's long-range planning doesn't support, or an external agency such as a credentialing or accreditation body requiring discontinuance. Even in these cases, a study must still be conducted if any three people (students, faculty members, or administrators) request one.

The passage names "The Age Discrimination Act of 1975" only in its section heading and does not explain what that law requires or how CSULB applies it. The text itself lists other laws the handbook covers, including Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, and other state and federal laws prohibiting discrimination, harassment, sexual misconduct, sexual exploitation, dating violence, domestic violence, stalking, and retaliation. This suggests the Age Discrimination Act is one of several laws referenced in CSULB's Title IX Resources Handbook (https://www.csulb.edu/sites/default/files/2026/documents/OEC%20-%20Title%20IX%20Campus%20Resources%20Booklet_7.%202026.pdf), but the passage gives no further detail about it.

Under the Policy on Discrimation, Harrassment and Retaliation (section 2.2.2), a Complainant initiates the Early Resolution process by contacting the Human Resources Manager. Once the concern is received, the Human Resources Manager will promptly meet with the Complainant to discuss it and, as appropriate, discuss reasonable interim remedies. If the allegation involves Sexual Misconduct, Dating or Domestic Violence, or Stalking, the Complainant will be advised to immediately file a Formal Complaint, because Early Resolution is not appropriate for those allegations.

Under section 6.2.1 of the Policy on Information Systems, once an investigation confirms a security breach involving notice triggering information, the CSULB Office of Information Security Management and Compliance must notify the Vice President of Administration and Finance and the Office of General Counsel. If the breach is large enough that a press release may be needed, that office also notifies the Senior Director, Information Security Management, the Associate Vice President, University Relations, and the Office of the Chancellor, with a copy to the CIO/Assistant Vice Chancellor. The office then confirms the breach to the responsible department and gives it advice and guidance. It also starts the campus breach notification process, working with the Executive Director or designee responsible for the breached equipment to handle the response and inquiries properly, and guides the employees designated to answer breach notification inquiries.

Under the Policy on Agency Accounts, any revenue generated by activities that are supported fully or partly by ASI fees must be deposited to and administered by the ASI Business Office. If the revenue fulfills a budgetary commitment, it goes into an ASI budget account. Otherwise, it is deposited into the organization's agency account. This provision appears as item 2.3 in the policy document available at https://asicsulb.org/corporate/documents/discover/policies/Policy%20on%20Agency%20Accounts%20103025.pdf.

The passage comes from the Engineering Controls section of the Policy on Hazard Communication Program, but it does not describe any specific engineering controls. Instead, it notes that personal hygiene is particularly important when handling highly toxic substances and that OSHA regulations prescribe hygiene practices for certain substances. It also describes labeling, required by the Hazard Communication Regulation, as an important control measure, but only if workers read, understand, and follow label instructions. The policy stresses that compliance with labels is an essential part of worker training and that workers should know what "danger," "warning," and "caution" mean and what to do when they see them.

Under California Education Code 67380(a)(1)(A), CSULB must compile records of all occurrences reported to campus police, campus security personnel, or campus safety authorities of, and arrests for, crimes committed on campus. These are crimes involving violence, hate violence, theft, destruction of property, illegal drugs, or alcohol intoxication. The university must make this information available within two business days when students, prospective students, employees, or the media request it. To request crime information, you can contact Chief John Brockie at john.brockie@csulb.edu.

The passage doesn't state any actual rules for the "Srwc - Bldgmnt" section of the Hazard Communication Program. It appears to be a fragment of a chemical inventory listing products such as Rust-Oleum aerosol topcoat paint, Sherwin-Williams Universal Acrylic Primer, lacquer thinner, disinfectant spray, and floor cleaner. It also lists manufacturers, dates (likely for safety data sheets), and storage or use locations like "Flam Cabinet," "SRWC - Rockwall," "SRWC - General Cleaning," and the Recycling Center. To find the actual requirements, you would need the full policy document at the cited source, https://asicsulb.org/corporate/documents/discover/policies/policy-on-hazard-communication-program.pdf.

Under CSULB Policy Statement 10-10, the candidate submits the entire research, scholarly, and/or creative work section of the RTP file to the Office of Faculty Affairs, which forwards it to each external evaluator. Each evaluator is asked to report on the quality and overall impact of the candidate's submitted materials on the discipline or profession, but not to recommend on the RTP action under consideration. The AVP for Faculty Affairs tells evaluators that their reports will be included in the candidate's RTP file and that the candidate will receive a copy. Every level of review treats these reports as additional evidence, weighed alongside all other evidence in the file.

According to ASI's Policy on Procurement, factors such as payment terms, product quality, compatibility with existing equipment, and delivery schedules can sometimes matter more than other considerations when choosing a vendor. As a recipient of federal funds, ASI is encouraged to make its best efforts to buy from "disadvantaged" businesses, including minority-owned, disabled veteran-owned, women-owned, and small businesses. ASI has local and statewide directories listing these businesses, and departments are encouraged to use them to find vendors. The ASI Business Office also purges the Supplier List annually of vendors ASI no longer does business with or chooses to avoid.

Under CSULB's Misconduct in Research & Creative Activity policy (PS 16-01), if there is a final finding of no Research Misconduct and the Respondent(s) request it, the RIO must make all reasonable and practical efforts to restore the Respondent's reputation. Depending on the circumstances and the Respondent(s)'s views, the RIO shall publicize the final outcome in any forum where the Allegation of Research Misconduct was previously publicized. Any institutional actions taken to restore the Respondent(s)'s reputation should first be approved by the DO.

Before any volunteer recruitment or assignment, a position description must be developed for each volunteer position and submitted to the Human Resources Office for review and approval. Each description must include the position's purpose and duties, a designated supervisor and worksite, a timeframe for the job, a list of qualifications, and a description of benefits. Descriptions should be reviewed and updated at least once a year, or whenever the work changes substantially. Each accepted volunteer receives the position description, which is then used in later management and evaluation, and the Human Resources Office is available to help staff develop volunteer jobs and descriptions.

This part of the handbook appears to be a contact listing rather than a policy explanation, and "W Broadway, Long Beach, CA 90802" looks like a partial street address with no street number. It is followed by police contact information: 911 for emergencies, (562) 435-6711 for non-emergencies, and the email LBPDSexCrimes@longbeach.gov, which suggests the address belongs to the Long Beach Police Department. The passage then lists the SAFER Campus Confidential Advocate, a confidential resource staffed by Jacqueline Urtez and Rocio Telumbre, reachable at (562) 985-4770 or SAFER@csulb.edu. It ends with a heading for Student Health Services – Behavioral Health Services but gives no details for that resource.

Under CSULB Regulation XII, students are generally individually responsible for any bodily injury, illness, or personal property loss or damage incurred while attending the University, and the University provides insurance only in specific situations. It provides medical insurance for students in NCAA team sports and obtains secondary medical insurance for registered sport club members, whose own health insurance is primary. Student travel accident insurance gives all CSU students, including those enrolled only in extended education programs, excess medical expense benefits while traveling to, from, or participating in University-sponsored activities away from campus. This accident-only coverage pays after any other health plan, excludes illness, disease, and treatment by CSU-employed or retained persons, and has a maximum benefit of $50,000 per covered person per accident.

Under PS 11-06, a dean may remove a department chair without faculty consultation, but only under extraordinary circumstances. These circumstances may involve issues such as department chair confidentiality, department chair misconduct, or University liability. Before requesting the chair's resignation or removing the chair, the dean must consult with the Provost and the Associate Vice President for Faculty Affairs.

Although the passage is titled "Repetition of Courses (PS 23-24)," its content actually concerns the college RTP policy, and its source link points to the University RTP Policy document. It states that the college RTP policy must specify in writing the standards for evaluating candidates in all three areas of evaluation, consistent with the university RTP policy, and must ensure consistency of standards across the college. Colleges are responsible for setting standards appropriate to the breadth of their disciplines. The policy must be ratified by a majority of voting tenure-track and tenured college faculty, approved by the dean and the provost, and regularly reviewed by the college's tenure-track and tenured faculty.

Under the Policy on Facilities Use, only authorized USU/SRWC staff may be in areas where set-up, teardown, repair, or maintenance is underway, and only those staff may set up events using facility furniture and equipment. All tables and chairs must be provided by the USU/SRWC. If an event needs specific equipment the facilities don't own, reasonable accommodation will be made with prior CEO approval, but the user pays all fees for acquiring it. USU/SRWC management decides how many staff each event needs, and all groups are charged for adequate staffing and service.

According to the CSULB Policies for CSULB Extension Programs, extension courses ordinarily will not be scheduled on campus. An exception is possible only where it can be clearly established that using campus facilities is essential. Even then, the extension course must not preempt or otherwise interfere with the regular instructional program. This guidance appears in the "Utilization of Campus Facilities" section of the policy, available at https://www.csulb.edu/academic-senate/policies-for-csulb-extension-programs.

Under the Policy on Agency Accounts, agency funds cannot be used to open or maintain off-campus or other unauthorized bank accounts. To enforce this, checks drawn on an agency account are never made payable to the organization itself or to any of its officers. The one exception is that a check may be made payable to an officer when it reimburses legitimate, documented organization expenses.

The passage doesn't describe CSULB's "General Policies" section as a whole. It covers only part of the Foundation's Gift Acceptance Policy (dated March 24, 2024), focusing on endowment funds. Gifts to endow a specific restricted purpose must be large enough to produce annual income that can fulfill the donor's purpose indefinitely. To protect the fund's integrity, only a "spendable" percentage of investment returns, set by Foundation Board policy, is assumed to be used, and the rest is reinvested. Endowment funds are managed by the Foundation's Board of Directors under the Foundation's investment and spending policies and California state law.

Under the ASI Policy on Banking, any funds handled on behalf of the ASI or its programs must be administered through bank accounts established in the name of the ASI or a CSULB Foundation. This policy implements Section 42403 of Title 5 of the California Code of Regulations, which requires that student body organization funds (except those from commercial services) be deposited in trust by the campus chief fiscal officer. All bank accounts in the ASI's name must be authorized in advance by the Associate Vice President for Financial Management. No ASI program, function, or activity may establish or maintain an off-campus bank account without prior authorization from ASI and prior approval from the Associate Vice President for Financial Management.

Under CSULB's Misconduct in Research & Creative Activity policy (PS 16-01), the Complainant is responsible for making Allegations in good faith and for cooperating with both the Inquiry and the Investigation. As a matter of good practice, the Complainant should be interviewed at the Inquiry stage and given the typed notes or recording of the interview for correction. During an Investigation, the Complainant must be interviewed and must be given the typed notes or recordings of the interview for correction.

The "Improper Transactions" section of ASI's Policy on Signature Authorization says that anyone granted signature authority must not knowingly prepare or approve a business transaction that is incorrect, inappropriate, fraudulent, or in violation of ASI policies on fraud, conflict of interest, or employee conduct. Anyone who knows of an improper transaction must report it immediately to the Executive Director, the Director of Administrative Services, or the ASI Treasurer. The policy also guarantees that there will be no retaliation against someone who reports a suspected improper transaction in good faith. For more on that protection, it refers readers to ASI's Policy on Whistleblower Protection.

Under CSULB's Federalwide Assurance, the university commits that whenever it engages in research covered by the Assurance, it will comply with the Terms of the Federalwide Assurance. Those Terms are not reproduced in the passage; they are in a separate document on the Office for Human Research Protections (OHRP) website. The passage is dated August 31, 2023, and its source is https://www.csulb.edu/sites/default/files/2024/documents/ORED%20FWA%202022.pdf.

Under the Policy on Injury and Illness Prevention Plan, accidents, injuries, illnesses, and "near-misses" are investigated using the procedures established in the plan, and their causes are identified and corrected. Employees are encouraged to report unsafe conditions and equipment or make safety suggestions, which the Human Resources Manager and the department supervisor evaluate, making corrections as necessary. Supervisors also regularly monitor their work areas and correct or report potential safety hazards.

Under PS 14-11, Bachelor of Arts and Bachelor of Science candidates meeting graduation requirements established during or after the 2013-14 academic year must complete exactly 120 units, including at least 40 upper-division units or their equivalent, unless the Chancellor grants an exception. Bachelor of Fine Arts and Bachelor of Music candidates under the same requirements must complete no fewer than 120 and no more than 132 units, or the limit set in Title 5, again unless the Chancellor grants an exception. Although the section is titled "Maximum Units Allowed in a Major," the passage itself sets total degree units rather than a specific cap on units within the major.

The passage, though labeled "Time, Place and Manner" under the "Program Structure" section, does not actually describe any program structure rules or requirements. It only lists support resources and their contact information. For students, these are the Bob Murphy Access Center for students with disabilities (Student Success Center 110, 562-985-5401) and CARES (Campus Assessment, Response & Evaluation for Students) at 562-985-4771 or CARES@csulb.edu. For employees, it lists the Faculty/Staff Assistance Program (562-985-7434) and LifeMatters by Empathia ((800) 367-7474). For the policy's substantive content, you would need to consult the full text at https://www.csulb.edu/university-policies/time-place-and-manner.

Under the "Use of Grant Funds" section of the Policy on Student Organization Grants, ASI-funded organizations must request reimbursement or payment from their ASI grants by completing the required forms. Those forms must be reviewed and signed by the organization's SLD advisor, and the request can proceed only with final approval from the AS Business Office. Reimbursement is allowed only when purchases clearly relate to the program description of an approved grant. This provision is labeled 10.1 in the passage, and the source is the 2026-27 Policy on Student Organization Grants document at https://asicsulb.org/corporate/documents/gov/2026-27%20Policy%20on%20Student%20Organization%20Grants%20(FINAL).pdf.

According to the Policy on Procurement (Credit Cards section), Budget Area Administrators who make frequent purchases may be issued an employer-sponsored, employee-liability credit card from American Express or Bank of America. For purchases under $1,000, the administrator may authorize the purchase directly with the vendor after getting prior approval from their immediate supervisor. The policy refers to Section 4.0 on Procurement Cards for further rules on purchase card use. Note that this passage comes from Associated Students, Inc. (asicsulb.org), so it may not reflect CSULB's university-wide policy.

The passage includes only one statement from the "Obscene Material" section: indecent or vulgar language is not considered obscene. This means crude or offensive wording alone does not make student media content obscene under the policy. The passage does not include the policy's actual definition of obscenity or any other details from that section. The rest of the excerpt covers a different topic, Section 2.2 on libelous or slanderous material.

Under the Policy on Volunteers, ASI recruits volunteers proactively to broaden campus community involvement, without regard to gender, disability, age, race, sexual orientation, or other protected status, and the standard qualification is suitability to perform a task for the organization. Student volunteers must maintain at least a 2.0 GPA each semester of service, must not be on probation of any kind, and must earn six units of course credit per semester (three units for graduate students), with additional requirements possible depending on the position. Volunteers may be recruited for a specific position or for a general interest in volunteering that is later matched to a specific function. Final acceptance of a volunteer cannot occur without a specific written volunteer position description for that person.

Under the Policy on Accounting, the Direct Payment Procedures (17.1.2) cover all payment situations not tied to a purchase order or contract, and invoices received by the Business Office are forwarded to the appropriate budget area contact to begin the process. Purchases must follow ASI guidelines and be allowable under the funding source; otherwise the invoice will not be paid, even if the goods were received, and the vendor will be told to seek payment from the individual who placed the order. The budget area must attach a completed Check Request, including the accounting distribution, to the original invoice and have it approved by the individuals on its Signature Authorization Card or Delegation of Authority Form. No payment may be approved unless the budget area has a current signature authorization record on file with the A.S. Business Office, where completed Check Requests are submitted for payment processing.

Under the Policy on Master's Degrees (PS 25-11), a graduate student in a master's program carries a full-time load at 8 units per semester, and the maximum load is 18 units per semester. A student who wants to exceed that maximum must first meet with their Graduate Advisor. If the advisor supports the request, the student submits an online extra unit petition, which requires approval from both the Graduate Advisor and the Associate Dean of the College. Separately, a student who wants to exceed the typical academic load for their program must discuss it with the Graduate Advisor, Department Chair, or Director.

Under CSULB's Regulation XVI, the section on criminal penalties for fraud and abuse in student financial assistance programs incorporates regulations adopted by the U.S. Congress. These regulations are the federal code related to Section 490 (Criminal Penalties) of the Higher Education Act of 1965. The passage does not describe the specific penalties, such as fines or prison terms, so those details would need to be checked in the full regulation at https://www.csulb.edu/student-affairs/campus-rules-and-regulations/regulation-xvi.

Under section 11.1 of the Policy on Information Systems, user access is granted to a specific individual and cannot be transferred to or shared with another user. Users must not share their password or user ID with anyone else. The policy states that this principle protects the integrity, security, and privacy of both the individual user account and the entire system.

Under PS 19-03, reassigned time releases faculty from other duties so they can pursue research, scholarly and creative activities (RSCA), while faculty small grants are monetary awards that can cover expenses such as student assistance, minor equipment, materials and supplies, or travel. Both are awarded competitively at the college level, using support allocated by Academic Affairs that colleges may supplement with their own funds. Awards may be reassigned time, small grants, or a combination, equivalent to the Vacant Rate for up to 6 WTU per academic year, and applications for more than 3 WTU require additional justification. If more than 3 WTU of reassigned time is awarded, the awardee may take it in one semester or spread it over two. College faculty councils set the application and evaluation criteria, procedures and deadlines, determine the composition and charge of the award committee, and may establish procedures for converting reassigned time into small grants and vice versa.

Under the Bylaws, a special meeting of the Board may be called by the Board Chair, the Chief Executive Officer, or any five directors, by delivering a written notice to the Board Chair or Chief Executive Officer. Notice and conduct of special meetings, like regular meetings, must follow the Education Code provisions governing California State University auxiliary organizations (Title 3, Division 8, Part 55, Chapter 7, Article 2, Section 89920 et seq.) or any later law that replaces them. The Board may also hold closed sessions during a special meeting, as permitted by California Education Code Section 89923.

Under CSULB's RTP policy (PS 23-24), all tenure-track and tenured faculty undergo performance review: tenure-track faculty are evaluated every year, and tenured faculty every five years. For tenure-track faculty, the first and second years of service involve a periodic review that gives feedback on progress toward tenure. That review is conducted by the department RTP committee, the department chair, and the college dean, though the first-year review may be done by just the chair and dean. In the third year, the evaluation becomes a reappointment review, and successful candidates are reappointed for one, two, or three years, followed by periodic or reappointment reviews in the fourth and fifth years as appropriate. These timelines apply to assistant professors appointed with no service credit and may vary with level of appointment and service credit.

Under the Policy on Signature Authorization, the Executive Director may revoke the signature authority of any Division Director or department supervisor under two conditions. The first is when the Executive Director and Treasurer determine that the signatory has engaged in an improper transaction as defined in the policy. The second is when they determine that the signatory lacks sufficient knowledge of the current policies, rules, laws, regulations, and other restrictions on the resources for which he or she has been delegated authority. Once revoked, signature authority may be reinstated only with the approval of the Executive Director and Treasurer.

The "Controlled Games" section explains that nonprofit organizations, including auxiliary organizations, may lawfully hold casino nights, poker nights and similar charitable fundraisers under California Business and Professions Code §19985-19987, provided both the nonprofit and any equipment or service suppliers submit an annual registration to the Bureau of Gambling Control 30 days before the event and check local police or sheriff requirements. Each nonprofit is limited to one such event per year, lasting no more than five hours, and only people over 21 may play. No cash prizes or wagers are allowed, though winners may receive donated prizes worth no more than $500 each, with a $5,000 cap on total prizes per event. At least 90 percent of gross revenue must go to the nonprofit, no more than 10 percent may compensate those running the event, and the games cannot be conducted online. The passage also begins a requirement to keep detailed records, but it is cut off before the details are given.

According to the ASI Bylaws 2025-26, each elected officer serves a term of no more than one year, ending on May 31. Each Board sets the term of office for these officers, subject to Senate approval. Officers may run for re-election an unlimited number of times, except the President, Executive Vice President, and Vice President of Finance, who are limited to two years in the same position. The strict prohibitions on using public funds and resources for political campaign activities apply to issues before voters, but they do not limit the CSU's ability to participate in the legislative process, and state resources may be used for legislative advocacy. At CSULB, stalking is defined under the CSU systemwide nondiscrimination policy, which replaced the former Executive Orders 1096 and 1097. Stalking means engaging in a course of conduct directed at a specific person that would cause a reasonable person to fear for their own safety or the safety of others, or to suffer substantial emotional distress. A "course of conduct" means two or more acts in which someone, directly, indirectly, or through third parties and by any method or device (including electronic means), follows, monitors, observes, surveils, threatens, or communicates to or about a person, or interferes with their property. Stalking is prohibited whether or not it is sexual in nature. Reports can be made to the campus Title IX/Equity and Compliance office or to University Police.

In policies modeled on the federal Uniform Guidance (2 CFR 200.331), a "contractor" is an entity that receives a contract from the university to provide goods or services for the university's own use in carrying out a sponsored project. A contractor is distinguished from a subrecipient. A contractor instead provides similar goods or services to many purchasers in a competitive setting, under normal business operations, and is not responsible for the project's programmatic decisions. CSULB's Financial Conflict of Interest policy implements federal Public Health Service regulations (42 CFR Part 50, Subpart F) and similar sponsor requirements to keep the design, conduct, and reporting of sponsored research free from bias caused by investigators' financial interests. Investigators, meaning anyone responsible for the design, conduct, or reporting of the research, must disclose significant financial interests related to their institutional responsibilities. Disclosure is required before submitting a proposal, at least annually during the award, and within 30 days of acquiring a new interest. A designated institutional official or committee, working through the Office of Research and Sponsored Programs, reviews the disclosures to decide whether a financial conflict of interest exists. If one does, the university creates and monitors a management plan, which may involve public disclosure, independent oversight, modifying the research, or divestiture, and reports the conflict to the funding agency as required. The policy also requires investigators to complete FCOI training before beginning funded work and at least every four years, and it allows sanctions and retrospective review when investigators fail to comply.

At CSULB, "initiation" falls under hazing rules, which prohibit any method of initiation or pre-initiation into a student organization that causes or is likely to cause bodily danger, physical harm, or serious psychological or emotional harm to a student or other person. This applies to all affiliated organizations, including fraternities, sororities, clubs, and athletic teams. The prohibition comes from the CSU Student Conduct Code (Title 5, California Code of Regulations, Section 41301) and California Penal Code Section 245.6 ("Matt's Law"). Neither the victim's consent nor the activity happening off campus is a valid defense. Violations can lead to student discipline up to expulsion, loss of recognition for the organization, and possible criminal charges, so check CSULB's Student Conduct and Ethical Development office for the current campus-specific procedures.

I can't recall the exact wording or policy number of CSULB's Policy on Student Media, so I can only describe how such provisions typically work. Student media policies at public California universities generally allow student editors broad freedom under the First Amendment and California Education Code Section 66301 but exclude material that is legally obscene. "Obscene" in this context is a narrow legal category, usually defined by the U.S. Supreme Court's *Miller v. California* test and California Penal Code Section 311: material that, taken as a whole, appeals to a prurient interest in sex, depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way, and lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. Content that is merely vulgar, profane, sexually frank, or offensive to some readers is generally still protected, so this kind of clause doesn't let the university censor content simply because it's distasteful. For the exact language, check the policy on CSULB's website or ask the Student Media office or the Office of Academic Senate.
